reason: Title invokes fraud-fighting but Medicaid bills frequently contain carve-outs, safe harbors, or eligibility tightening disguised as administrative efficiency. Without summary text, the 'STOP FRAUD' framing is a classic regulatory capture tell—accusatory language often masks provider exemptions or beneficiary-access restrictions.
vectors: Entitlement erosion: potential Medicaid eligibility narrowing or benefit cuts hidden under anti-fraud rhetoric
Regulatory capture: likely safe harbors or exemptions for specific provider classes (managed care, pharmaceutical, hospice)
Fiscal bleed: possible DSH/GME carve-outs or payment-reform mechanics that redirect federal flows
title: STOP FRAUD in Medicaid Act

reason: Pharmacy benefit manager (PBM) regulation is a classic regulatory capture audit vector: PBMs operate as opacity-enforcement intermediaries between payers, pharmacies, and patients. Any 'requirements' language without explicit price-transparency or margin-ceiling mandates likely creates safe harbors or carve-outs that entrench PBM market power while appearing pro-competitive.
vectors: regulatory_capture: PBM exemptions or 'safe harbor' definitions that protect spread pricing or formulary control
market_access_exploit: rules that consolidate PBM gatekeeping (e.g., credentialing, network access standards that favor large PBMs)
fiscal_bleed: Medicare/ERISA 'administrative cost' pass-throughs that shift cost burden to beneficiaries while protecting PBM revenue
entitlement_erosion: formulary restrictions or step-therapy mandates that reduce drug access for Medicare/Medicaid enrollees under guise of 'requirement'
title: To amend title XVIII of the Social Security Act, and the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974, to create certain requirements with respect to pharmacy benefit managers.
